findings.claim: The tolerance fix narrows the required random-offset property to pixel centres, removing coverage where the stricter tolerance is hardest to meet. Restore that coverage or obtain an explicit contract amendment for the finite-precision limitation.
findings.evidence: Commit 1ae554b replaces continuous st.floats offset strategies and zero-axis examples with integer pixel indices. Current lines 579-585 restrict round trips to the 55×55 grid, excluding zero axes and all coordinate magnitudes below 25 m. Lines 593-605 check only finiteness for tiny offsets at general centres. This weakens the previous test domain while AC5 remains unchanged; PRD.md:1548 prohibits weakening tests to make them pass.

resolution.reason: Escalated: this needs a human decision on a threshold and its scope (PRD 7 Tolerances, PRD 23.7). It is the same issue as codex2-r2-1 in reviews/T3-02-codex-2-r2.json. The finding is right that the property test now samples only D29 pixel centres, and that offsets below 25 m at general centres get finiteness checks only. But that coverage cannot be restored at rtol 1e-10, atol 1e-12 m with float64 output, so the choice is a contract amendment. Evidence (scratch scripts, not committed; uv run --locked python with mpmath 1.4.1 at 40 digits): 9,000 continuous offsets at random centres (|lat0| <= 1.4 rad, |lon0| <= 3 rad; 1,000 per body and domain). For each offset, every float64 (lat, lon) pair within +-3 ulps of the exact inverse was put through an exact forward. No pair meets rtol 1e-10, atol 1e-12 m on both x and y in 103, 153 and 295 of 1,000 cases (Moon, Mars, Earth) with |x|, |y| <= 14 m; in 538, 677 and 800 with |x| <= 1 m and |y| <= 2,500 m (offsets near an axis, far from the origin); and in 1 of 1,000 for each body with offsets uniform over the whole 5 km window. The best pair misses by up to 705 times the allowance. geometry.py fails exactly those cases: there are 0 cases where it fails and some float64 pair passes. The cause is float64 resolution, not the evaluation. A float64 longitude near lon0 moves x in steps of R cos(lat) ulp(lon0), up to 2.8e-9 m on Earth, and a latitude in [1, 2) rad moves y in steps of 1.4e-9 m. The allowance for a component near 0 is 1e-12 m. Restoring the domain would therefore only add a test that no implementation can pass. Leaving it out removes no input that a correct float64 implementation could get right. D29 evaluates the inverse only at pixel centres, where every component is at least 25 m and the round trip passes. Options for the human: (a) amend AC5 to random centres and random D29 pixel centres, as the test does now; (b) for continuous offsets, apply the tolerance to x/W and y/W, reading PRD 7 "normalized float64 fixtures" as round 1 first did; (c) approve a float64 floor term for continuous offsets, for example atol + rtol*|v| + R*ulp(pi); (d) on continuous offsets, check each direction separately: the inverse against the exact (lat, lon) within a stated number of ulps, and the forward of each returned float64 point against the exact forward of that same point at rtol 1e-10, atol 1e-12 m. A scratch run of (d) on 12,000 continuous offsets found the inverse within 1.9 ulps of exact and the forward at most 3.3e-4 of the allowance. Recommendation: (a), optionally with (d) as added coverage. Background is in story notes decision (3).
